 NYC’s pied-à-terre tax can move forward, appeals court rules
 By Aaron Ginsburg 
 November 5, 2026 
 Credit: Diane Picchiottino on Unsplash 
 New York City has won an appeal in a challenge to the rollout of its pied-à-terre tax, marking a victory for one of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s key agenda items. A state appeals court on Wednesday ruled that the Mamdani administration can continue rolling out the tax, reversing a September ruling by a Staten Island judge who said the city had mishandled the program’s launch and must redo it. While the lawsuit challenged the program’s rollout, not the tax itself, the surcharge still faces two ongoing lawsuits seeking to strike down the program.
 Pitched by Mamdani as a way to fulfill his pledge to “tax the rich,” the surcharge applies to secondary one- to three-family homes valued at more than $5 million, as well as secondary condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more, as 6sqft previously reported .
 The now-dismissed lawsuit, filed by a group of homeowners in early August, stemmed from reports that some individuals with only one primary New York City residence received notices that they may be subject to the tax, creating what the plaintiffs called “mass confusion” surrounding the surcharge.
 The confusion was amplified when the city’s Department of Finance published its twice-yearly report listing the names and addresses linked to nearly one million properties, as required under the new law.
 After clarifying that the release fulfilled a state law requirement and covered most non-rental residential properties in the city, not just those likely to be subject to the surcharge, Mamdani later extended the deadline for submitting documentation twice.
 Following the Staten Island judge’s September ruling that the administration must redo the program’s rollout, Mamdani immediately filed an appeal. With Wednesday’s legal victory, the city faces one fewer legal challenge. 
 The appeals court ultimately found that property owners “lacked standing” to sue because they had not experienced any “concrete or definable injury” from the program’s rollout. Additionally, the court found that the confusion cited by homeowners following the supplemental list’s release was “too generalized, tenuous, and ephemeral” to constitute a “cognizable injury-in-fact.”
 Randy Mastro, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the New York Times that it was unclear whether the homeowners planned to appeal the court’s decision. However, in a statement, he continued to lambast the tax rollout, calling it “lawless and chaotic” and saying it would go “unremedied.”
 Mastro also said he believed the two other ongoing legal challenges to the program, which challenge the constitutionality of the surcharge itself, would be successful.
 In a statement to The Hill , Mamdani celebrated the legal victory and committed to defending against the two remaining lawsuits.
 “From day one, those with the most have attempted to use every legal avenue available to shield their wealth and avoid contributing more to our city,” Mamdani said. “We are heartened by the Appellate Division’s ruling in the City’s favor, and we will continue working with our partners in Albany to defend this law against the ongoing challenges in Suffolk County.”
 The first of the other lawsuits, filed by Stephen Wynn, founder of Wynn Resorts, and former U.S. Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross and his wife, Hilary Geary Ross, argues that the tax discriminates against wealthy out-of-towners. Wynn and the Rosses all live in Florida but own second homes in NYC, according to the Times.
 Filed by the corporation that owns the Upper East Side co-op building known as The Montclair , as well as several homeowners, some of whom live in Florida and Suffolk County, the second lawsuit makes a similar challenge. The lawsuit is backed by the Real Estate Board of New York.
 Officials say the tax could generate up to $500 million in additional revenue annually, although that figure has been questioned by City Comptroller Mark Levine. In a May report , Levine said that exclusions for rental units and “behavioral responses” to the tax could lower the actual revenue to between $340 million and $380 million.

 Brooklyn’s DeKalb and Lafayette Avenues getting major bus and bike lane upgrades 
 By Aaron Ginsburg 
About 18,000 Brooklyn bus riders can soon expect faster service as the city breaks ground on a redesign of DeKalb and Lafayette Avenues. Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Department of Transportation (DOT) Commissioner Mike Flynn on Thursday announced the start of work on the project, which aims to speed up service for daily riders of the B38 bus. The project will redesign DeKalb Avenue from Broadway to Flatbush Avenue and Lafayette Avenue from Ashland Place to Patchen Avenue, adding 2.7 miles of new offset and curbside bus lanes, protected bike lanes, and other street safety improvements.

 NYC subway saw over 3.1 million riders on Marathon Sunday, busiest in MTA history 
 By Aaron Ginsburg 
The New York City subway carried 3.14 million riders during the New York City Marathon last weekend, setting a new record for Sunday ridership. Gov. Kathy Hochul and the MTA on Monday announced the milestone, which coincided with the 50th anniversary of the event's five-borough race that closes roads across the city and encourages New Yorkers and visitors alike to use public transit. The November 1 total surpasses the previous Sunday record of 2.8 million riders last year.

 By Aaron Ginsburg 
Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday threatened to sue federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) unless its agents immediately stop using city-owned property as staging grounds for its operations. The mayor sent a letter to the Trump administration demanding that ICE cease its “illegal” use of city-owned lots for immigration enforcement operations, arguing that the activity endangers New Yorkers and “sows fear” among those seeking to access city property.  Upper East Side movie theater Cinema 123 by Angelika has closed after 60+ years 
 By Devin Gannon 
Manhattan's East Side has lost another movie theater. Cinema 123 by Angelika closed on Thursday after more than 60 years on the Upper East Side. Reading International, the owner of the theater, agreed to sell the property in September for $41 million. The closure follows the announcement that an AMC theater in Kips Bay would shutter by the end of the year.

 Brooklyn gets its first on-street trash containers for apartment buildings 
 By Aaron Ginsburg 
Brooklyn's first residential on-street trash containers were installed on Thursday in the city's latest effort to get rid of piles of trash on sidewalks. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced that Brooklyn Community District 2 will receive 700 on-street trash containers, known as Empire Bins, with full containerization targeted for completion by the end of fall. The announcement follows Mamdani’s April plan to expand the program to six additional community districts and builds on the success of a pilot in West Harlem, which became the first neighborhood in North America to containerize its trash in June 2025.

 City will redesign Sunset Park’s deadly Third Avenue 
 By Aaron Ginsburg 
Nearly two months after a nurse was killed by a hit-and-run driver, a notoriously dangerous stretch of Third Avenue in Sunset Park is set for a major redesign. On Wednesday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced that the Department of Transportation will overhaul a 2.1-mile stretch of the avenue next year, from 62nd to 20th Streets, with pedestrian islands, improved intersections, and protected bike lanes. The plan responds to years of calls from Sunset Park residents for street safety improvements following multiple fatal traffic incidents, demands that failed to move forward under former Mayor Eric Adams’ administration.

 NYC wants your input on plans to create 40 miles of greenways in the outer boroughs 
 By Aaron Ginsburg 
New Yorkers are being invited to weigh in on the city’s plans to create more than 40 miles of greenways across the outer boroughs. Department of Transportation (DOT) Commissioner Mike Flynn on Monday announced that the planning process for four greenways in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Staten Island, and southern Queens will begin this fall. Residents interested in shaping the projects can attend a series of workshops. The first workshop, focused on the Bronx greenway, is slated for November 4.

 Central Park breaks ground on new $35.7M stormwater system 
 By Aaron Ginsburg 
Work began this week on a $35.7 million project to reduce flooding across Harlem by improving stormwater management in northern Central Park. Gov. Kathy Hochul, Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and the Central Park Conservancy on Monday broke ground on the North End Recirculation Project, which will ease pressure on the combined sewer system serving the park and surrounding neighborhoods while conserving the city’s drinking water supply. Slated for completion in fall 2028, the project is expected to divert 132 million gallons of water from local sewers and save 175 million gallons of drinking water annually.
